comparison: Perfect agreement on background claims (C1, C20, C21). Both evaluations accept these as valid context establishing the need for improved voluntary THC consumption models. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on E-gel overcoming aversive responses (C22-C30, C84-C87). Both evaluations confirm chocolate flavoring enables higher THC consumption. OpenEval emphasizes statistical support (ANOVA p<0.001), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the finding with direct quotes.

Agreement on dose-dependent cannabimimetic responses (C2-C3, C33-C45). Both evaluations accept the behavioral triad findings and CB1R dependence. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation, peer reviewers confirm behavioral effects and antagonist validation without challenge.

Disagreement on interpretation of temporal dynamics and aversive memory (C4, C46-C52, C56, C89-C91). OpenEval supports the aversive memory inference as reasonable. Peer reviewers explicitly critique this, noting the abstract implies chronic utility but data shows consumption reduction after multiple days, questioning model utility beyond acute measures.

Agreement on pharmacokinetic findings (C5-C6, C58-C62, C68, C95, C99). Both evaluations accept THC and 11-OH-THC accumulation data and brain levels. OpenEval notes parallel accumulation as novel; peer reviewers confirm measurable brain levels without challenge.

Disagreement on sex differences in pharmacokinetics (C101). OpenEval supports the claim as documented. Peer reviewer explicitly requests clarification, noting prior studies show stark sex differences in PK and asking for separate male/female profiles, indicating insufficient documentation.

Agreement on sex-dependent acoustic startle effects (C7-C8, C76-C80). Both evaluations accept the biphasic i.p. response and male-specific E-gel effects. OpenEval notes marginal correlation significance; peer reviewers accept findings without concerns.

Disagreement on dose-prediction model validation (C9, C82-C83). OpenEval supports the model's generalization to acoustic startle with close agreement between predicted and measured responses. Peer reviewer raises significant concern about modeling error, questioning how predicted 30 mg/kg i.p. dose is possible when that dose wasn't tested and would likely produce near-zero startle.

Agreement on dose-prediction methodology and temporal dynamics (C69-C74, C92-C94). Both evaluations accept the approach correlating behavioral responses between routes. OpenEval notes sound methodology with acknowledged variability; peer reviewers confirm time-dependent findings without challenge.

Agreement on sex differences in consumption and cannabimimetic responses (C31-C32, C88). Both evaluations accept the minimal sex differences with appropriate statistical testing. OpenEval notes one exception at 1 mg dose; peer reviewers note inclusion of both sexes as strength.

Agreement on lack of sex differences in THC triad (C39-C40). Both evaluations accept these findings. OpenEval notes vehicle effect on locomotion; peer reviewers accept sex comparisons without challenge, noting inclusion of both sexes as study strength.

Disagreement on chronic utility claims (C103-C107). OpenEval supports these as appropriately framed possibilities with translational relevance. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, explicitly stating the model's utility for chronic consumption 'remains to be determined' and questioning whether it will be useful beyond acute measures.

Agreement on temporal relationships (C53-C55, C57). Both evaluations accept the parallel time courses between consumption, brain levels, and behavioral effects. OpenEval emphasizes statistical support; peer reviewers note temporal monitoring as study strength.

Agreement on lack of PK-behavior correlation (C66). Both evaluations accept this negative finding without challenge. OpenEval notes it weakens mechanistic inferences; peer reviewers do not question the finding.

OpenEval rates mechanistic hypothesis about dual THC/11-OH-THC contribution (C96-C98) as uncertain due to speculation and lack of correlation with behavior. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific mechanistic claims.

OpenEval rates mechanistic hypotheses about higher 11-OH-THC levels and declining responses (C100, C102) as uncertain, noting they are speculative and not experimentally validated. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports acknowledgment of SR1 experiment limitation (C43) regarding anorectic effects as appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific methodological limitation.
